questions.subject: BIOLOGY

It makes the molecule nonpolar and hydrophobic
It makes the molecule acidic by donating a proton
It stores energy in high-energy phosphate bonds

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why DNA contains deoxyribose instead of ribose.

answer.exemplar: Deoxyribose lacks a hydroxyl on the 2' carbon, making DNA more chemically stable for long-term genetic storage than RNA.

questions.explanation: The missing 2' hydroxyl reduces reactivity, helping DNA resist degradation. RNA uses ribose for more versatile, shorter-lived roles.

Substrate shape is irrelevant to catalytic activity
Enzymes are consumed during the reaction and must match
The active site shape complements the substrate

questions.explanation: Enzyme specificity arises from active site shape and chemical complementarity. Enzymes are not consumed and do not bind all molecules equally.

Both catalyze reactions as enzymes
Both transmit genetic information

Saturated fats because straight chains pack tightly

It is a phospholipid with two tails and a head

Carboxyl group, lipid tail, glycerol, and nitrogen base

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A map note asks what stabilizes protein alpha helices; which answer is correct?

options.text: Covalent peptide bonds between side chains
options.misconception: confuses backbone bonds with stabilizing forces

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups
Disulfide bridges between cysteine residues
Ionic bonds between charged R groups
options.misconception: confuses side-chain interactions with backbone H-bonds

questions.explanation: Alpha helices are stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen. Disulfide and ionic bonds stabilize higher-order structure.

Denaturation strengthens peptide bonds
Denaturation converts proteins into lipids
Denaturation disrupts higher-order structure but not peptide bonds

questions.explanation: Denaturation unfolds a protein by disrupting secondary, tertiary, or quaternary structure, but peptide bonds remain intact. Hydrolysis, not denaturation, breaks peptide bonds.

options.misconception: confuses activation energy with total energy

options.text: Enzymes make reactions thermodynamically favorable
Enzymes lower the activation energy required
Enzymes add energy to products after the reaction

questions.explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy, increasing rate without changing total energy or thermodynamic favorability. They do not add energy to products.

It is a substrate consumed in every reaction
It inhibits the enzyme permanently
It is a product released by the enzyme

pH has no effect on enzyme shape
Enzymes function equally well at any pH
Each enzyme is adapted to its physiological environment

questions.explanation: Pepsin works best in acidic stomach conditions, while trypsin works best in alkaline small intestine. Enzyme structure adapts to environment.

questions.stem: A map calculation uses an enzyme with Km 5 mM at substrate concentration 5 mM; what fraction of Vmax is the reaction rate?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A map note describes an inhibitor resembling substrate; which inhibition is this?

options.text: Noncompetitive inhibition binding an allosteric site
Competitive inhibition competing for the active site
Uncompetitive inhibition binding only the enzyme-substrate complex
Irreversible inhibition destroying the enzyme permanently

questions.explanation: A substrate-like inhibitor competes for the active site, defining competitive inhibition. Noncompetitive, uncompetitive, and irreversible inhibition differ in binding site or permanence.
questions.hint: Substrate mimic competes for active site.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct an error about noncompetitive inhibition
questions.stem: A report says noncompetitive inhibition can be overcome by adding more substrate; identify the error.

options.text: Noncompetitive inhibition increases Vmax
Noncompetitive inhibition only affects small substrates
Noncompetitive inhibition cannot be overcome by adding substrate
Noncompetitive inhibition is identical to competitive inhibition

questions.explanation: Noncompetitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site and reduce Vmax without changing Km, so adding substrate does not overcome them. Competitive inhibition can be overcome by substrate.
questions.hint: Allosteric binding is not competed by substrate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY

Competitive inhibition by a substrate analog
Denaturation of the enzyme by heat
Activation of the enzyme by its product

questions.explanation: Feedback inhibition uses an end product to inhibit an early enzyme, preventing overproduction. It is not competitive inhibition, heat denaturation, or activation.
questions.hint: End product regulates its own synthesis.

Misfolding always increases protein activity

questions.stem: Explain why ATP is called the energy currency of the cell.

answer.exemplar: ATP stores energy in its phosphate bonds and releases usable energy when hydrolyzed, powering many cellular processes.

questions.explanation: ATP acts as a transferable energy source because hydrolysis releases energy that drives cellular work. It is continuously regenerated.

questions.stem: A map table shows a protein at pH below its pI; what is its net charge?

options.text: Net negative charge
No net charge
Net charge depends only on size
Net positive charge

questions.explanation: Below the pI, protonation gives the protein a net positive charge. At pI, net charge is zero; above pI, it is negative.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A map calculation starts with Vmax 100 units and a noncompetitive inhibitor reduces it by 40 percent; what is the new Vmax?
questions.explanation: A 40 percent reduction from 100 leaves 60 units. The new Vmax is 60.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Final map entry asks which patterns are common protein secondary structures; which is correct?

options.text: Only primary peptide sequences
Alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets
Only quaternary subunit assemblies
Only denatured random coils
options.misconception: confuses native secondary with denatured state

questions.explanation: Common secondary structures include alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets, stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonds. Primary, quaternary, and denatured coils are different concepts.
